Calf
kăf
n. (the young of the herd; the idol of Sinai and of Bethel; rendering Hebrew egel, ben baqar, Greek moschos)
From Anglo-Saxon cealf. In Scripture the calf is both the best thing a host can kill for a guest and the worst thing a nation ever made for itself.

Biblical Definition

Calf runs the full range from hospitality to apostasy. Abraham, entertaining three strangers, “ran unto the herd, and fetcht a calf tender and good” (Gen 18:7) — the costliest quick meal a herdsman could offer. Israel at Sinai takes the same animal and makes it a god: Aaron “fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel” (Exo 32:4). Note the exact form of the sin. They did not renounce the LORD or credit another deity with the exodus; they attributed His work to an image, and Aaron proclaimed a feast to the LORD the next day. It is a violation of the second commandment, not the first — the true God worshipped by a means He forbade. Moses grinds it to powder and makes them drink it (Exo 32:20), and the LORD plagues the people “because they made the calf, which Aaron made” (Exo 32:35) — a sentence that will not let the leader hide behind the crowd.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a calf as the young of the cow, and notes the golden calf of Scripture as an idol set up by the Israelites — also the calves of the lips, that is, praise.

expand to see more

CALF, n. plu. calves. The young of the cow kind, or of the bovine genus of quadrupeds.

2. In contempt, an ignorant, stupid person; a dolt.

3. The thick fleshy part of the leg behind.

The golden calf, an idol set up by Aaron and the Israelites at Horeb.

Key Scripture

Exo 32:4 — "And he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt."

Exo 32:35 — "And the LORD plagued the people, because they made the calf, which Aaron made."

Gen 18:7 — "And Abraham ran unto the herd, and fetcht a calf tender and good, and gave it unto a young man; and he hasted to dress it."

Exo 32:20 — "And he took the calf which they had made, and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it."

Modern Corruption

Idolatry imagined as the worship of a rival god, when Exodus 32 shows the far commoner sin — the true God worshipped by means He never appointed, with His own name attached to it.

expand to see more

The golden calf is the definitive biblical case of will-worship, and its details are usually softened. Israel did not say here is a new god. They pointed at a calf and credited it with the exodus the LORD had performed, and Aaron announced “to morrow is a feast to the LORD” over it. The name was right; the means were invented; and the LORD sent a plague. That is why the regulative principle is not fussiness. Sincere worship of the true God through an unappointed medium is exactly what Sinai punished.

Exodus 32:35 deserves the last word in this entry, because of its strange doubled phrasing: the people were plagued because they made the calf, which Aaron made. The people made it and Aaron made it. Neither is permitted to hide behind the other — not the congregation behind the leader who gave them what they demanded, nor the leader behind the congregation that demanded it. Aaron's excuse in verse 24, that he threw in the gold and there came out this calf, is one of Scripture's most recognizable evasions.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew egel (H5695), a calf — the Sinai and Bethel idols; ben baqar, a son of the herd — Abraham's calf; Greek moschos (G3448), a calf — the fatted calf of Luke 15.

expand to see more

Hebrew egel (H5695) — a calf; the molten calf of Exo 32:4 and Jeroboam's two calves at Bethel and Dan (1Ki 12:28).

Hebrew ben baqar — a son of the herd; the tender and good calf Abraham killed for his guests (Gen 18:7).

Greek moschos (G3448) — a calf, young bull; the fatted calf killed for the returning prodigal (Luk 15:23).

Usage

"“These be thy gods, O Israel” — the LORD's work credited to an image."

"“Because they made the calf, which Aaron made” — neither hides behind the other."

"“A calf tender and good” — the same animal, offered rather than worshipped."
